Why it matters: One of NASA's nine Artemis III candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole (Oct 2024 list)
Surface temperature: Diviner (LRO) ground surface: maximum about 320 K (47 °C) toward the ridge's upper elevations, about 220 K (-53 °C) near its base. Summit averages about 180 K in summer and 130 K in winter. Long-lit polar spots in general: about -50 ± 10 °C
Terrain: Mountain massif with about 1,250 m of relief; candidate landing area slope 5.6° ± 2.0°; a candidate landing spot is a relatively flat area above a 5,000 m cliff
Ice and water: Near permanently shadowed regions that may hold water ice
Earth sites that match parts of it (sugg: Kamil and Lonar (craters); Harrat Khaybar (basalt, tubes); East Antarctic Plateau (cold, partly)
Sources: LROC mosaic center (https://data.lroc.im-ldi.com/lroc/view_rdr/NAC_ROI_MALAPERTLOD); Astronomy (https://www.astronomy.com/space-exploration/here-are-the-nine-sites-where-artemis-3-might-land-on-the-moon/); Wueller et al. 2025 (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2025JE009127); Diviner max temps (arXiv 2303.03911) (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.03911); Air & Space (https://www.airspacemag.com/daily-planet/new-light-on-the-lunar-poles-156800678/); Universe Today (https://www.universetoday.com/articles/heres-where-artemis-iii-might-land-it-looks-inviting); NASA Moon fact sheet (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html)

Why it matters: Ice-rich northern plain; SWIM's pilot study region; proposed landing site for robotic and crewed missions
Surface pressure: 6.36 mb average (4.0 to 8.7 by season), under 1% of Earth's
Surface temperature: Not measured here. Proxy only: at the Viking 1 lander site, AIR temperature 1.6 m above the ground ranged -89 to -31 °C over a day (NASA fact sheet). Not a ground temperature
Terrain: Flat plain of lava flows up to 3 billion years old; yardangs; dust devils seen by Mars Express
Ice and water: Shallow ground ice; excess ice widespread in the mid-latitudes
Sources: ESA Mars Express (https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Mars_Express/Earth_tones_on_Mars); SWIM (https://swim.psi.edu/); NASA JPL (https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/where-should-future-astronauts-land-on-mars-follow-the-water/); Arcadia Planitia (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcadia_Planitia); NASA Mars fact sheet (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html); Viking weather sensors (https://arcnav.psi.edu/urn:nasa:pds:context:instrument:met.vl2)

Why it matters: Where lunar ice is expected; the coldest surfaces, for comparison
Surface temperature: Parts of Haworth crater never exceed about 40 K (-233 °C)
Ice and water: Surfaces below 110 K can trap water ice for over a billion years
Earth sites that match parts of it (sugg: None on Earth comes close (see Earth's limits)
